titre: Only the Dead Have Seen the End of War
accroche: In 1962, General MacArthur quotes Plato before the West Point cadets for a sentence one reads in Santayana in 1922
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1962, General Douglas MacArthur delivers his farewell address to the corps of cadets at West Point. According to the article Wikipedia devotes to George Santayana, this speech contains the sentence “only the dead have seen the end of war,” credited to Plato. The article makes it an early example of an attribution to Plato that has become frequent, adding in parentheses a cautious reservation: “if it is indeed a mistake.” What remains to be seen is where the sentence is actually read, word for word.

## A Philosopher Born in Spain, Dead in 1952

The sentence appears in George Santayana, an American philosopher, essayist, poet, and novelist of Spanish origin: born in Spain, he left for the United States at the age of eight and died on September 26, 1952. Wikipedia ranks him among authors of aphorisms and cites, alongside “Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it,” precisely this one: “Only the dead have seen the end of war.”

It is read in chapter 25, titled “Tipperary,” of *Soliloquies in England and Later Soliloquies*, a collection published in New York in 1922 by Scribner's. The full text is online: the sentence there is exactly “Only the dead are safe; only the dead have seen the end of war,” that is: only the dead are safe, only the dead have seen the end of war.

## What the Chapter Tells

The chapter opens on the bells of the Armistice. They teach Santayana nothing: a week earlier or later, he writes, they had to ring. In the streets of Oxford, flags are hung here and there, and in a café, wounded officers, come from a hospital in Somerville, sing the old tune of *Tipperary*.

Santayana watches them and is severe: the poor boys think themselves safe, they think the war, “perhaps the last of all,” is over. It is then that he writes the sentence. He adds at once that non-being does not deserve the name of peace: it is by an illusion of contrast that one is tempted to call it that.

The sequel goes further than the maxim. To live in peace with things, Santayana judges, one would have to make peace with the fact of war, and it is the stupid obstinacy of self-love that produces tragedy. The chapter ends on an image: as long as the world turns, one will see Tipperary only through the window of a troop train, and the world has a long way to go.

## What This Shifts

Quoted alone, the sentence reads as a warning about the war that ends only with death. In the chapter, it answers officers convinced that the war is over, and it is immediately qualified: death is not peace. Detached from the text, it loses this nuance.

The sources of this entry do not say why Plato's name became attached to the sentence, or who, before MacArthur, credited it to Plato. They establish two things: the sentence is written, word for word, by Santayana in 1922, and it is credited to Plato in a 1962 speech.

quiz.question: According to the entry's sources, where does the sentence “only the dead have seen the end of war” come from?
choix: It was written by MacArthur for his 1962 speech
It is read in Santayana, in a text published in 1922
It dates from 1952, the year of Santayana's death
No text earlier than the 1962 speech contains it
quiz.explication: The sentence is read word for word in the chapter “Tipperary” of Soliloquies in England, published in 1922: it is the earliest text the entry cites. Wikipedia notes that MacArthur's speech (1962) credits it to Plato, forty years after the 1922 publication, and Santayana died in 1952.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which chapter of Soliloquies in England and Later Soliloquies is the sentence about the dead and the end of war read?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The sentence is read in chapter 25, titled Tipperary, of the collection published in 1922: it is there that Santayana writes it, on emerging from the bells of the Armistice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to this chapter, where do the wounded officers Santayana watches singing in an Oxford café come from?
choix: From the town of Tipperary in Ireland
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The chapter says they come from a hospital in Somerville, and sing the old tune of Tipperary in an Oxford café, at the bells of the Armistice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Just after writing that only the dead have seen the end of war, what nuance does Santayana add?
choix: That non-being does not deserve the name of peace
That one should rejoice at the Armistice without reservation
That this war will truly be the last of all
That Plato was right to say it before him
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Santayana writes that non-being does not deserve the name of peace, and that it is by an illusion of contrast that one is tempted to call it that.
